\begin{problem}[CP-II-0016] \label{prob:cp-ii-0016} \textbf{Sequence Convergence.} Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence of continuous real-valued functions on $[0,1]^k\subset\mathbb{R}^k$, and suppose that $f_n \Rightarrow f$ uniformly. Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in $[0,1]^k$ with $x_n\to x$. \par\noindent\textbullet\quad Show that $f_n(x_n)\to f(x)$. (Uniform convergence preserves sequential continuity.) \par\noindent\textbullet\quad Is (a) still true if $f_n$ converges pointwise, but not necessarily uniformly, to $f$? Uniform convergence means $\sup_{y\in[0,1]^k}|f_n(y)-f(y)|\to 0$. If each $f_n$ is continuous and $f_n\Rightarrow f$ uniformly, then $f$ is continuous. \end{problem}

\begin{problem}[CP-II-0023] \label{prob:cp-ii-0023} \textbf{Integral Estimate.} Let $F:[a,b]\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be continuous, $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $R>0$. Suppose that \[ \sup_{[a,b]\times \overline{B_R(x_0)}}\|F\|\le \frac{R}{b-a} \quad\text{and}\quad \|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|\le K\|x-y\| \] for some $K$ and all $t\in[a,b]$, $x,y\in\overline{B_R(x_0)}$. We showed in lecture that for each $t_0\in[a,b]$ there is a unique $f\in C([a,b];\overline{B_R(x_0)})$ solving \[ f(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F\big(s,f(s)\big)\,ds,\qquad t\in[a,b]. \] Show that this $f$ is in fact the unique function in $C([a,b];\mathbb{R}^n)$ solving the integral equation. \setlength{\itemsep}{6pt} \par\noindent\textbullet\quad (Picard--Lindel\"of / Gr\"onwall) If $F$ is continuous in $t$ and Lipschitz in $x$, the integral equation has a unique solution as long as the solution stays in the domain. \par\noindent\textbullet\quad A uniform bound on $\|F\|$ controls how far a solution can move away from $x_0$ by integrating the bound. \end{problem}

\begin{problem}[CP-II-0041] \label{prob:cp-ii-0041} \textbf{Differentiability.} (a) Let $B=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be the closed unit ball and $F:[0,1]\times B\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be continuous. Suppose there is $K>0$ with \[ \|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|\le K\|x-y\|\qquad \forall\,t\in[0,1],\ \forall\,x,y\in B. \] Given $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n$, by Picard--LindelĂ„â€šĂ‚Â¶f there exist $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and differentiable $f_1,f_2:[0,\varepsilon]\to B$ such that $\dot f_j(t)=F(t,f_j(t))$ and $f_j(0)=x_j$ for $j=1,2$. Show that \[ \|f_1(t)-f_2(t)\|\le \|x_1-x_2\|\,e^{Kt}\qquad (0\le t\le\varepsilon). \] (b) Now assume a HĂ„â€šĂ‚Â¶lder condition: there are $K>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with \[ \|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|\le K\|x-y\|^\alpha\qquad \forall\,t\in[0,1],\ \forall\,x,y\in B. \] Show for the same $f_1,f_2$ that \[ \|f_1(t)-f_2(t)\| \le \Big(\,\|x_1-x_2\|^{1-\alpha}+(1-\alpha)Kt\,\Big)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}} \qquad (0\le t\le\varepsilon). \] What does this imply about the set of solutions to $\dot f=F(t,f(t))$, $f(0)=x_0$ on some interval $[0,\varepsilon]$? \bigskip \hrule \bigskip \setlength{\itemsep}{6pt} \par\noindent\textbullet\quad \textbf{GrĂ„â€šĂ‚Â¶nwall (differential form).} If $u\ge0$ is absolutely continuous and $u'(t)\le Ku(t)$ a.e., then $u(t)\le u(0)e^{Kt}$. \par\noindent\textbullet\quad \textbf{Osgood / generalized GrĂ„â€šĂ‚Â¶nwall.} If $u'(t)\le Ku(t)^\alpha$ with $0<\alpha<1$, then $u(t)^{1-\alpha}\le u(0)^{1-\alpha}+(1-\alpha)Kt$. \bigskip \end{problem}

egin{problem}[CP-II-0075] \label{prob:cp-ii-0075} 	extbf{Norm Comparison.} Equivalent Norms and Their Topologies Let $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ be two norms on a vector space $X$. Show that the following are equivalent: \par
oindent	extbullet\quad The norms are equivalent: $\exists a,b>0$ such that $a\|x\|_1\le\|x\|_2\le b\|x\|_1$ for all $x\in X$; \par
oindent	extbullet\quad The topologies induced by $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ are the same; \par
oindent	extbullet\quad The convergent sequences are the same for both norms. Each norm induces a metric $d_i(x,y)=\|x-y\|_i$ and hence a topology. Two norms are called \emph{equivalent} if there exist constants $a,b>0$ with $a\|x\|_1\le\|x\|_2\le b\|x\|_1$ for all $x$. Then both norms yield the same open sets, convergence, and continuity. Conversely, identical convergence or topology implies the existence of such $a,b$. \end{problem}

oindent	extbullet\quad Show that there exists a constant $C>0$, depending only on $n$, such that \[ \sum_{\substack{g\in\mathbb{Z}^n \ \|g\|_1\le K}}  rac{1}{(1+|g|)^{n+1}} \;\le\; 1 + C \sum_{k=1}^K  rac{1}{k^2} \] holds for all $K\in\mathbb{N}$. \begin{problem}[CP-II-0562] \label{prob:cp-ii-0562} \textbf{Sequence Convergence.} Suppose $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $(f_i)_{i=0}^\infty$ with $f_i:A\to\mathbb{R}^m$ be a sequence of functions.
